title: Could you spot it?
intro: 12 real-looking messages. For each one, decide: scam or legit? Every message is made up, but each is built the way real ones are. You get the answer and the tell right after each pick.

tiers.name: Scam-proof
tiers.line: 12 for 12. Scammers would skip you. Now make sure the people you love score this well.

tiers.name: Sharp eye
tiers.line: You caught almost everything. Look back at the one or two that got you: that's the kind a scammer would send you.

tiers.name: Getting there
tiers.line: You spotted the obvious ones. The rest is about three habits: slow down, don't use their link or number, and never read a code to anyone.

tiers.name: Prime target
tiers.line: Scammers win on rush and trust, and they'd have caught you a few times here. The good news: the same three tells cover most of these.

questions.message: You have an unpaid toll of $6.89. Pay today to avoid a $50 late fee and a hold on your license: tollpay-center.com/pay
questions.tell: Tiny bill, big threat, strange link
questions.why: A small amount plus a scary penalty and a deadline is the classic unpaid-toll text. Check your toll account by typing your agency's real site yourself, never through the link.

questions.message: Your First Harbor sign-in code is 482913. We will never call, text or email to ask for this code. (You just tried to sign in.)
questions.tell: You asked for it, and it asks nothing of you
questions.why: A code you just requested, with no link and no request, is normal. If a code ever arrives when you didn't sign in, don't share it: someone may have your password, so change it.

questions.message: We stopped a $1,240 charge on your card. To reverse it, please read me the 6-digit code we just texted you.
questions.tell: They want the code read back
questions.why: That code is the key to your account, and the caller is using it to sign in as you. Hang up and call the number on the back of your card.

questions.message: Your payment failed. Update your card within 24 hours or your account and saved profiles will be deleted. [Update payment]
questions.why: The sender's address isn't the company's real domain, and the deadline is there to rush you. Open the app or type the site yourself to check your billing.

questions.message: Hi Grandma it's me!! Lost my phone so this is my new number. Can you help me with something? Don't tell Mom yet
questions.tell: New number, a favor, and secrecy
questions.why: A new number, a request coming next, and "don't tell" is how family-emergency scams start. Call your grandchild's old number, or a parent, before you reply.

questions.message: Your prescription is ready for pickup at your usual store on Elm St. Reply STOP to opt out of texts.
questions.tell: No link, no payment, no personal details asked
questions.why: It tells you something you can check in person and asks you to do nothing risky. A message turns suspicious when it adds a link to "confirm" or asks you to pay.

questions.message: Hi! Loved your profile. Remote role, $450/day, just liking videos for brands. Start today! There's a $99 refundable training deposit.
questions.tell: Easy money, then you pay first
questions.why: Real employers don't charge you to start, and "liking videos" for big pay is the task-job scam. The deposit is never refunded, and more fees follow.

questions.message: IRS: You are owed a tax refund of $1,382.40. Claim within 48 hours: irs-refund-claim.org
questions.tell: A surprise refund link from "the IRS"
questions.why: The IRS doesn't make first contact by email or social media, and only texts people who signed up for its messages. Check refunds on IRS.gov with the Where's My Refund tool, typed in yourself.

questions.message: I'll take the couch and pay with Zelle. It says you need a business account, so send $300 to upgrade and I'll pay you back with the couch money.
questions.tell: A buyer who needs you to pay first
questions.why: Payment apps don't make sellers pay to receive money. The "upgrade" email that follows is fake too. A real buyer pays you; you never send money to sell something.

questions.message: New sign-in to your account from Chrome on Windows, Tuesday 9:14 am. If this was you, you don't need to do anything. If not, open the app and go to Security.
questions.tell: It sends you to the app, not to a link
questions.why: A sign-in alert that asks for nothing and points you to the app is normal. If it wasn't you, follow it in the app or on the site you type in, not from an email button.

questions.message: WARNING! Your computer is infected with 5 viruses. Do not close this window. Call Support now at 1-888-555-0143.
questions.tell: A security warning with a phone number
questions.why: Real security warnings never ask you to call a phone number. Close the browser tab (or restart the browser) and don't call.

questions.message: Your bill for February is $84.20, due March 3. Pay at the website on your previous bills, by mail, or by calling the number on the back of this bill.
questions.tell: Normal amount, normal due date, your usual ways to pay
questions.why: It matches what you expect and lets you pay the way you always do. The scam version is a call or knock saying your power gets cut off within the hour unless you pay by gift card or app.
